description: Multi-dimensional adversarial review of a diff or capability: correctness, security, and spec compliance, with every finding adversarially verified before it is reported.

findings.title: Child task view shows the original WRONG verdicts next to a re-evaluated CORRECT state
findings.evidence: After this slice, `TaskProgress.state` reads `effectiveCorrect`, so a re-evaluated attempt 1 changes the task to CORRECT_FIRST_TRY. But `outcome()` still builds the parts from `latest.parts.map { PartOutcome(it.key, it.verdict, it.normalized, null, it.locked) }`, which are the original verdicts. It also picks `progress.latest`, which can be attempt 2 (originally wrong, the one that triggered the reveal). So `TaskView.lastResult` can show `state = CORRECT_FIRST_TRY` together with WRONG per-part verdicts, and the tutor feedback is computed from the new state. Design decision 8 says practice state everywhere reads the re-evaluated verdict, but the per-part feedback was not updated to match.
findings.suggestion: When the attempt has a primary-scope `reevaluation`, overlay `reevaluation.verdicts` onto the part verdicts in `outcome()`. When the task was resolved by re-evaluating an earlier attempt, show that attempt (or the state-determining one) rather than `progress.latest`. Add an IT covering 'reevaluate attempt 1 of a REVEALED task, then GET the task view'.

findings.title: Zero-XP re-evaluation writes no ledger row, so startup reconciliation later pays a TASK award from a different attempt
findings.evidence: `onReevaluation` inserts the REEVALUATION row only `if (amount > 0)`. A task that was UNRESOLVED (no TASK row) and is improved to resolved with an award of 0 (possible when `config.minimum` is 0 and hints cost all the XP) gets no row. `taskAwarded` then stays false, and `reconcile()` on the next startup inserts a TASK award tied to `progress.latest` and that attempt's hints. That attempt may not be the one the re-evaluation resolved, so the ledger records the resolution against the wrong attempt and hint count.
findings.suggestion: Always insert the REEVALUATION row when the task had no task XP before (amount 0 is allowed by the `BETWEEN 0 AND 1000` check). Alternatively, have `reconcile` skip tasks whose resolution comes from a re-evaluated attempt.

findings.title: Flag queue listing does N+1 full task loads (all parts, specs converted) only to build an 80-char excerpt
findings.evidence: `list()` maps every report through `view`, which calls `catalog.task(report.taskId)` and `store.attempt(id)` per report. `ContentCatalogService.task` loads the whole task and runs `it.spec.toChecker()` on every part, but only `prompt` is used here. With no paging (design decision 6), the queue grows by two or more queries per report on every list.
findings.suggestion: Add a batch lookup to `ContentCatalog`, e.g. `prompts(taskIds): Map<UUID, String>`, plus `PracticeStore.attempts(ids)`. Build the views from those maps, or join the attempt in the `reports()` query.

findings.title: Re-evaluation that cannot grade (shape mismatch / unreadable) returns the same 200 changed=false as 'still wrong'
findings.evidence: `val grade = if (parts.isEmpty()) null else ReevaluationRules.regrade(parts, attempt)`. A null or Unreadable grade then falls into `decision == ReevaluationDecision.NoChange` and returns `ReevaluationOutcome(false, XpOutcome.NONE, view(report), null)`. The admin cannot tell 'the fixed spec still rejects the answer' from 'the stored input no longer fits the task's parts (e.g. part type changed or deleted)'. In the second case, re-trying after more spec edits will never help. This matches design decision 7, but the admin never learns why nothing happened.
findings.suggestion: If the contract allows, add a reason to `ReevaluationResult` (or a distinct 409 detail) when the attempt cannot be graded under the current parts. Otherwise, record this as an open question in the docs store.

findings.title: Flag queue is unpaginated and makes 2 extra queries per report, while anyone on the LAN can create reports without logging in
findings.evidence: The child report endpoint needs no login and has no rate limit. `PracticeService.report` (PracticeService.kt:201-212) adds a `problem_report` row on every call. Any device on the home LAN, or a child repeatedly tapping 'report', can create thousands of reports for a served task. The new admin `GET /api/admin/reports` (AdminStatsController.listReports → FlagQueue.list) loads every report with no limit. `view()` (ProgressStats.kt:141) then runs `catalog.task()` and `store.attempt()` for each one, so the admin page gets slow and the real reports are lost in the noise. This is not a confidentiality or integrity issue: re-evaluate and dismiss are behind the admin session plus CSRF chain (`/api/admin/**`, AdminSecurityConfiguration.kt:71-79), and `attemptId` is set by the server (PracticeService.kt:210-211), so it cannot be used for IDOR.
findings.suggestion: Add a limit/offset (or a cap) to `PracticeStore.reports`. Fetch the task excerpts and attempts for the listed reports in one batch query each instead of one query per report. Put a simple limit on report creation on the child side, e.g. at most N OPEN reports per task, or a short per-task cooldown.

findings.title: Coverage summary: 67 backend-applicable scenarios: 64 implemented, 3 partial, 0 missing, 0 contradicted
findings.evidence: I mapped the store spec contract/openspec/specs/progress-stats/spec.md (60 scenarios, minus 'Child UI has no stats', which is frontend-only, and the UI-only halves of 'No data yet' and 'Topic with no resolved tasks') and the change delta (7 scenarios) to code and tests. Each requirement has an implementation and a test: StatsRules.sessions/weeks/metricMet/firstTry (practice/domain/Stats.kt), FlagQueue.list/reevaluate/dismiss (practice/application/ProgressStats.kt:89-150), AdminStatsController (weeks/status/reportId validation), and V6__progress_stats.sql (append-only attempt_reevaluation, REEVALUATION ledger kind with a unique index per report). The tests are StatsRulesTest (23 cases incl. DST and the Sunday-midnight session), ProgressStatsIT (12), FlagQueueIT (21 incl. 401/403/404/409/400 paths) and PracticeLogCaptureIT (NFR-3). The 5 Attempt-log scenarios (FR-42) were delivered by slice 7 and are only re-exposed here. The OpenAPI boundary matches: 4 operations, the documented 200/400/401/403/404/409 codes, no extra fields. FR-40 and FR-41 (backend+frontend in the plan) are both traced in the specs and tests.
findings.suggestion: None. This entry is the coverage line the output contract asks for; the partial items are listed separately.

findings.title: taskPromptExcerpt trims trailing whitespace before the ellipsis, which differs from design decision 6; the field has no store-spec requirement
findings.evidence: design.md decision 6: "`taskPromptExcerpt` = the first 80 code points of the task's current Czech prompt, with `…` appended when cut." Code: `return prompt.substring(0, prompt.offsetByCodePoints(0, EXCERPT_LENGTH)).trimEnd() + "…"`. If code point 80 falls on whitespace, the excerpt is shorter than 80 code points. The FlagQueueIT test (`excerpt.removeSuffix("…").length shouldBe 80`) uses a prompt with no whitespace near the cut, so it cannot catch this. The store spec's Flag queue requirement only says each entry shows "the task". The 80-code-point excerpt (and the new public ContentCatalog content query that serves it) exists only in OpenAPI and design.md.
findings.suggestion: Either amend design decision 6 to say trailing whitespace is trimmed, or drop `.trimEnd()`. Add a test whose prompt has a space at code point 80. Consider adding the excerpt to the store spec's Flag queue requirement so this scope drift is documented.

findings.title: A replay re-evaluation only counts as better when the whole attempt becomes correct; a per-part improvement is not covered by the spec
findings.evidence: Store spec: "If the new verdict is better than the attempt's recorded verdict, it is recorded alongside the original, the report becomes `FIXED`, and 0 XP is awarded; otherwise nothing changes." Code: `val wasCorrect = attempt.reevaluation?.correct ?: attempt.correct; return if (!wasCorrect && grade.correct) ReplayCorrected else NoChange`. On a multi-part replay attempt, a fix that turns one WRONG part CORRECT while another part stays WRONG is per-part better, but it returns NoChange and the report stays OPEN. The V6 migration comment also assumes "a recorded re-evaluation is always all-correct". ReevaluationRulesTest and FlagQueueIT only cover single-part replays.
findings.suggestion: Amend the store spec to define "better" for a replay attempt as "the attempt is now correct as a whole" (matching the code and the design note). Add a two-part replay test where only one part is fixed and assert changed=false.

findings.title: The 'Rank-up from a re-evaluation' scenario is only partly tested: the 'celebration plays once' half is not asserted
findings.evidence: Scenario: "THEN HQ shows the 2nd rank and the rank-up celebration naming the 2nd rank plays once." The test checks `hq.read<Int>("$.rank.index") shouldBe 1` and `hq.read<Int>("$.pendingRankUp.index") shouldBe 1`. It never acknowledges the rank-up (`/api/child/hq/rank-up-ack`) or checks that a second HQ read returns no pendingRankUp. The one-shot behaviour comes from slice 8, but nothing checks it for a rank-up crossed by a REEVALUATION ledger row with no attempt_id.
findings.suggestion: Extend the test: call rank-up-ack and then assert `$.pendingRankUp` is null on the next HQ read.

result.reasoning:
I confirmed the problem in the code, and it doesn't depend on unusual timing.

1. **State uses the corrected verdict.** In `TaskProgress.state` (Rules.kt:20-27), attempts 1 and 2 are judged by `effectiveCorrect`. That property (Model.kt:87) returns the re-evaluated verdict for a first play-through attempt, if an admin recorded one.

2. **Per-part results use the original verdict.** `outcome()` builds the parts from `latest.parts.map { PartOutcome(it.key, it.verdict, …) }` (PracticeService.kt:344), which is the verdict stored when the child answered. Nothing in this path applies `reevaluation.verdicts`.

3. **`latest` is just the last attempt.** It is `attempts.lastOrNull()` (Rules.kt:33), not the attempt that now decides the task's state.

4. **Re-evaluation is how the mismatch arises.** `ReevaluationRules.decide` stores a re-evaluation exactly when the new verdict improves the outcome (Reevaluation.kt:60-68).

So there are two realistic ways for the task view (`screen` → `lastResult`, PracticeService.kt:325) to contradict itself:
- **Attempt 1 wrong, then corrected by the admin.** The state becomes CORRECT_FIRST_TRY, while the latest attempt (attempt 1, or attempt 2 if the task was already revealed) still shows its WRONG parts.
- **Attempt 2 of a revealed task corrected.** Even here, where `latest` is the corrected attempt, the state becomes CORRECT_SECOND_TRY but the parts still come from the original WRONG verdicts.

The tutor feedback is computed from the new state (line 347), so it will also disagree with the per-part verdicts.

Nothing guards against this: re-evaluations only apply to the first play-through, and `screen` uses that scope whenever no replay run is active, which is the normal case after an admin re-evaluation. A child opening the task after an admin accepts their report will hit this. It's a confusing display, not a security or data-integrity problem, so "major" is about right, perhaps slightly high.

The finding depends on `config.minimum` being 0, and that can't happen. `GamificationConfigParser.kt:47` parses every XP key with a lower bound of 0, except `minimum`, which gets a lower bound of 1 (`if (key == "minimum") 1 else 0`). The XpConfig doc comment also says "minimum 1..1000", and the shipped `gamification.json` sets `"minimum": 1`.

`XpRules.taskAward` returns `maxOf(config.minimum, …)` for every resolved state (CORRECT_FIRST_TRY, CORRECT_SECOND_TRY and REVEALED), so any resolved state earns at least 1 XP no matter how many hints were used. In the finding's scenario the task had no TASK or REEVALUATION row, so `taskXp` is 0. That makes `amount = taskAward(resolved) - 0 ≥ 1`, so the `if (amount > 0)` branch always runs and a REEVALUATION row is inserted.

`JdbcXpLedger.taskAwarded` counts both `TASK` and `REEVALUATION` rows, so `reconcile()` later sees the task as awarded and skips it. The finding's 'zero-XP re-evaluation of a previously unresolved task' can't happen with any configuration the parser accepts. The `amount > 0` guard only skips the case where the task already had task XP at or above the new award, and there `taskAwarded` is already true. The mechanism doesn't hold.

The finding depends on `config.minimum` being 0, and that can't happen. `GamificationConfigParser.kt:47` checks every XP key against 0..1000 except `minimum`, which must be 1..1000 (`if (key == "minimum") 1 else 0`). The `XpConfig` KDoc says the same ("minimum 1..1000"), and the shipped `gamification.json` uses minimum 1.

`XpRules.taskAward` (domain/Gamification.kt:39-41) returns `maxOf(config.minimum, ...)` for every resolved state (CORRECT_FIRST_TRY, CORRECT_SECOND_TRY, REVEALED). So any resolved state gets an award of at least 1.

Take the claimed scenario: the task had no TASK or REEVALUATION row, so `ledger.taskXp(taskId) == 0`. Re-evaluation then improves it to a resolved state. The amount is therefore `taskAward(...) - 0 >= 1 > 0`, so the `if (amount > 0)` guard at line 96 always inserts the REEVALUATION row. `taskAwarded` treats any non-MISSION_BONUS row for the task as awarded, so it becomes true and `reconcile()` will not add a second TASK award.

The amount can only be 0 when task XP was already paid. In that case `taskAwarded` is already true and reconcile skips the task anyway. A real user or admin can't reach the claimed path with a valid configuration.

I could not refute the mechanism; the code does what the finding says. `FlagQueue.list` (ProgressStats.kt:94) runs `store.reports(status).map(::view)`. `view` (ProgressStats.kt:141-142) calls `catalog.task(report.taskId)` and `report.attemptId?.let(store::attempt)` once per report. `ContentCatalogService.task` (ContentCatalogService.kt:30-38) loads the whole task through `tasks.find` and maps every part through `it.spec.toChecker()`. `view` then uses only `.prompt` for the 80-code-point excerpt. Nothing batches or caches these calls; the class's `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` does not combine separate repository lookups. So a list costs 1 + up to 2N queries plus unnecessary spec conversions.

This is an efficiency problem, not a correctness one. The output is still right: the excerpt, the attached attempt and the status filter all come out correctly. The app is single-user with one child, so the report queue should stay small, and the cost is linear and bounded. The finding is accurate but belongs under performance or maintainability, so I'd lower its severity rather than call it refuted.

The mechanism is real. `FlagQueue.list` (ProgressStats.kt:94) maps every row from `store.reports(status)` through `view` (line 141–142). For each report, `view` calls `catalog.task(report.taskId)` and, when the report has an attempt, `store.attempt(id)`. `ContentCatalogService.task` (ContentCatalogService.kt:30–38) runs `tasks.find(taskId)`, which is a per-id SQL query in JdbcTaskStore.kt:62 and may load more for the task's child data. It then builds a `CatalogPart` with `it.spec.toChecker()` for every part. `view` uses only `.prompt`. `store.attempt` is a separate `WHERE a.id = ?` query (JdbcPracticeStore.kt:193). I found no `@Cacheable` and no batching anywhere. `reports()` takes no paging parameters, so every list call costs 1 + about 2N queries for N reports.

Exploitability is negligible, though. This is an admin-only endpoint in a single-child tutoring app. Reports come from one child flagging tasks, so the queue will realistically hold tens of entries, not thousands. An attacker can't grow the queue without being that child, and can't call the listing without admin rights. The codebase already accepts this per-id pattern elsewhere (MissionService.kt:103, `ids.distinct().mapNotNull(tasks::find)`). The finding is also filed under the wrong dimension: this is a performance issue, not a correctness one, and it never produces a wrong result.

Verdict: the mechanism is confirmed and reproducible, but the real-world impact is close to zero. Downgrade it to a nit or optional optimization.

The finding is refuted. The code does what the finding describes, but that is the specified behaviour, not a correctness defect. At `ProgressStats.kt:111-114`, an empty parts list gives a null grade, and a null or Unreadable grade falls into `NoChange || grade !is Grade.Graded`. That returns `ReevaluationOutcome(false, NONE, view(report), null)`. Nothing is persisted and the report stays OPEN. The design calls for exactly this. Design decision 7 (design.md:78-80) says: "If the stored input no longer fits a part's shape ... or any part is unreadable under the new spec, nothing changes." The Risks section (design.md:178-179) repeats it: "handled as 'no change' whenever the stored input cannot be graded." The finding itself admits the code "matches design decision 7". No state is corrupted, no XP is wrong, and no error is swallowed. The report stays OPEN, so the admin can still dismiss it or fix the spec and retry. The missing reason field is a suggestion to change the API contract (`ReevaluationResult`). That is a docs-store change and a UX/diagnostics request, not a wrong mechanism in this code. The finding's own confidence is low.

The mechanism is real and reachable. In `ProgressStats.kt:105-115`, `parts` comes from the task's current content. If `parts` is empty (task or parts deleted), `grade` is null. `ReevaluationRules.regrade` (`Reevaluation.kt:42`) also returns null when `Grading.shapeErrors` is not empty, for example after an admin switches a part between choice and text. `Grading.grade` returns `Grade.Unreadable` when the stored raw input is UNPARSEABLE under the edited spec. In every one of these cases `ReevaluationRules.decide` returns `NoChange` (line 55), and the service returns `ReevaluationOutcome(false, NONE, view(report), null)`. That response looks exactly like a genuine "regraded, still wrong / not improved" result. The report stays OPEN and nothing tells the admin why.

An admin can trigger this with ordinary actions: edit a task's part type or remove a part, then press re-evaluate. No attacker is needed. Nothing is exploitable, though. There is no security, data-integrity or XP impact, because nothing is written. The outcome is the "nothing changes" result that the design requires: `openspec/changes/implement-progress-stats-api/design.md` decision 7, lines 78-80, and the Risks section, lines 178-179. The code matches the contract exactly, so this is not a code bug. The real problem is that the API cannot tell the two cases apart, and fixing that needs a docs-store change to `api/openapi.yaml`, not a backend patch. The finding is correct on the facts and already concedes it matches the design. Verdict: not refuted, but downgrade it to a contract/UX open question (info level) rather than a correctness defect.

I could not confirm a correctness defect, so I'm marking this refuted.

What the code does: `Reevaluation.kt:56-58` returns `ReplayCorrected` for a replay attempt only when it was wrong before (counting any earlier re-evaluation) and is now correct as a whole. Otherwise it returns `NoChange`.

Why that is not wrong:
1. **The design matches the code.** `design.md` decision 8 says: "Replay attempt: … If the attempt was wrong and is now correct, the new verdicts are recorded, the report becomes FIXED…". The code follows this word for word.
2. **The spec's "verdict" means the whole-attempt verdict.** The store spec (progress-stats, lines 353-358) talks about "the attempt's recorded verdict". The same spec uses verdict at attempt level elsewhere, e.g. line 362 "attempts 1 and 2 were both `0,5` and marked `WRONG`". The spec never defines an order between per-part verdict vectors. Reading "better" as WRONG → CORRECT for the attempt is the natural reading, not a deviation.
3. **The replay rule follows the primary-scope rule.** For primary attempts, "better" is decided on the task outcome (`TaskProgress`), and that outcome only changes when the attempt as a whole becomes correct. A per-part improvement changes nothing there either.

The finding's own suggestion is to amend the spec to match the code. It doesn't claim the code misbehaves against any defined requirement. At most this is a wording ambiguity in the spec plus a missing two-part test, which is a test-coverage nit, not a correctness bug in this code.

The behaviour the finding describes is real. At `Reevaluation.kt:56-58` a replay attempt counts as improved (`ReplayCorrected`) only when the whole attempt goes from not-correct to correct (`!wasCorrect && grade.correct`). If a fix turns one part of a multi-part replay attempt from WRONG to CORRECT while another part stays WRONG, the result is `NoChange` and the report stays `OPEN`. Nothing elsewhere handles this case. The tests only cover single-part replays (`ReevaluationRulesTest` around line 125).

It is not clearly a spec violation, though. Store spec `progress-stats` lines 353-358 say "If the new verdict is better than the attempt's recorded verdict". Every scenario uses "verdict" for the whole attempt: WRONG → CORRECT at lines 74-76, 384-388 and 398-400. On that reading, a partly fixed attempt is WRONG before and after, so nothing is "better" and the code complies. rejected.title: Zero-XP re-evaluation writes no ledger row, so startup reconciliation later pays a TASK award from a different attempt
rejected.evidence: `onReevaluation` inserts the REEVALUATION row only `if (amount > 0)`. A task that was UNRESOLVED (no TASK row) and is improved to resolved with an award of 0 (possible when `config.minimum` is 0 and hints cost all the XP) gets no row. `taskAwarded` then stays false, and `reconcile()` on the next startup inserts a TASK award tied to `progress.latest` and that attempt's hints. That attempt may not be the one the re-evaluation resolved, so the ledger records the resolution against the wrong attempt and hint count.

`XpRules.taskAward` returns `maxOf(config.minimum, …)` for every resolved state (CORRECT_FIRST_TRY, CORRECT_SECOND_TRY and REVEALED), so any resolved state earns at least 1 XP no matter how many hints were used. In the finding's scenario the task had no TASK or REEVALUATION row, so `taskXp` is 0. `JdbcXpLedger.taskAwarded` counts both `TASK` and `REEVALUATION` rows, so `reconcile()` later sees the task as awarded and skips it. The finding's 'zero-XP re-evaluation of a previously unresolved task' can't happen with any configuration the parser accepts. The `amount > 0` guard only skips the case where the task already had task XP at or above the new award, and there `taskAwarded` is already true. The mechanism doesn't hold.
